enrichment.short_title: Medical negligence claim after fatal cardiac arrest
key_facts: Susan Mellor died aged 43 on 1 January 1998 from cardiac arrest en route to hospital after a history of hypertension and ischaemic heart disease.
Her widower claimed GPs failed to diagnose ischaemic heart disease in time and that cardiologist Dr West negligently discharged her on 13 January 1997.
Post mortem showed pulmonary oedema secondary to hypertensive and ischaemic heart disease with significant coronary artery disease.
The trial examined multiple consultations from 1992 to 1997 and expert cardiology evidence on diagnosis, referral and treatment pathways.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Clinical negligence trial in the Queen's Bench Division against GPs and Sheffield Teaching Hospitals NHS Trust.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed against all defendants; no breach or causation proved against Dr Groves or Dr Richards; Dr West found negligent in discharging Mrs Mellor but causation not established against the NHS trust.
enrichment.ratio: Even where a cardiologist breached duty by discharging a patient prematurely, the claimant must still prove on the balance of probabilities that timely diagnosis and treatment within the routine NHS timetable would have prevented death; here Mrs Mellor's underlying cardiac disease meant no defendant could have avoided the tragedy by due diligence.
legal_issues: Whether GPs breached duty in failing to diagnose ischaemic heart disease and refer to cardiology
Whether Dr West negligently discharged Mrs Mellor in January 1997
Whether any breach caused Mrs Mellor's death

enrichment.short_title: Coca-Cola D&O reinsurance claims control clause
key_facts: RSA reinsured its 21.5% participation in Coca-Cola's directors and officers liability cover under Lloyd's slip policies incorporating a standard Claims Control Clause.
Two US securities class actions were notified to RSA on 30 December 2000 but RSA did not advise reinsurers until 19 January 2001, outside the 72-hour cable notice period.
Reinsurers argued 'loss' in the CCC meant actual losses of third-party claimants against Coca-Cola, triggering the notice obligation when RSA received the complaints.
RSA argued 'loss' meant loss to Coca-Cola and its D&Os, and that complaints alleging inflated share prices did not give knowledge of actual loss.
enrichment.procedural_posture: One-day Commercial Court trial for declarations on reinsurers' indemnity obligations under D&O reinsurance contracts.
enrichment.outcome: RSA entitled to reinsurance indemnity; 'loss or losses' in the CCC refers to actual losses of third-party claimants, but RSA did not have actual knowledge of such losses before 19 January 2001 and was not in breach of the notice condition.
enrichment.ratio: In a liability reinsurance with a Claims Control Clause, 'loss or losses which may give rise to a claim under this policy' refers to actual (not alleged) financial losses of third-party claimants against the original insured; however, where loss depends on disputed underlying facts—such as whether share prices were artificially inflated—receipt of pleadings alone does not give the reinsured actual knowledge of actual loss.
legal_issues: Whose 'loss or losses' triggers the 72-hour notice obligation in the Claims Control Clause
What constitutes actual knowledge of loss as opposed to alleged loss
Whether the contra proferentem rule applies to standard CCC wording
Interaction of Full Reinsurance Clause and Daugava/Gan limitation principles

enrichment.short_title: Restricted patient recall and mental disorder classification
key_facts: The claimant killed his girlfriend in 1991, was found not guilty by reason of insanity, and was later conditionally discharged from Ashworth Hospital in March 2001.
He was recalled in February 2004 after concerns about drug abuse, a concealed relationship with a vulnerable 17-year-old, and behaviour mirroring pre-offence patterns.
Psychiatrist Dr Croy reported he no longer had mental illness but did have psychopathic disorder warranting inpatient treatment.
The claimant argued continued detention was unlawful because recall and prior tribunal classification had been on the basis of mental illness, not psychopathic disorder.

enrichment.short_title: Illegality defence to wrongful dismissal claim after tribunal finding
key_facts: Soteriou worked for Ultrachem from 1987 to 2000, maintaining he was self-employed while later claiming employee status for unfair dismissal.
An Employment Tribunal found his contract unenforceable due to illegality after he had represented to the Inland Revenue that he was self-employed.

enrichment.short_title: Housebuilding bricklayers as Working Time Regulations workers
key_facts: Redrow engaged bricklayers Wright and Roberts under standard 'Official Order' subcontract terms for residential housebuilding sites.
The tribunals found they were 'workers' under Regulation 2(1)(b) entitled to paid holiday under Regulation 14.
Redrow argued Condition 6 of its standard terms contemplated delegated labour and negated any personal obligation to perform work.
In practice each bricklayer performed work personally and was paid individually rather than through a gang leader.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal appeal from Employment Appeal Tribunal dismissals of Redrow's appeals against two Employment Tribunal decisions.
enrichment.outcome: Appeals dismissed; bricklayers were workers because, on the facts, Condition 6 did not apply and the parties intended a personal obligation to perform bricklaying work.
enrichment.ratio: Under Regulation 2(1)(b), whether an individual is a 'worker' depends on contractual obligation to perform work personally; where standard terms are a 'menu' governed by an 'insofar as applicable' clause, tribunals may exclude inapplicable conditions by reference to the factual matrix, and payment to individual bricklayers strongly indicates personal service obligations.

enrichment.short_title: Contributory locus to oppose public interest winding-up petitions
key_facts: The Secretary of State petitioned to wind up Rodencroft Ltd, W G Birch Developments Ltd and H-M Birch Ltd on public interest grounds alleging asset-stripping fraud by disqualified director Simon Allso.
Mrs Registrar Derrett made winding-up orders without hearing Allso's evidence, holding he lacked locus standi to oppose.
Allso controlled Rodencroft but was not a shareholder of the other two companies, whose shares were held by his associates or nominees.
The petitions alleged use of companies to acquire distressed targets, extract management fees, and leave creditors unpaid.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from registrar's ex parte public interest winding-up orders under section 124A Insolvency Act 1986.
enrichment.outcome: Appeals dismissed for Birch Developments and H-M Birch; appeal allowed for Rodencroft with petition remitted for full hearing on merits; Allso must demonstrate solvency to oppose as contributory.
enrichment.ratio: A contributory may appear and oppose a Secretary of State section 124A petition even where the company itself does not oppose, but only if he demonstrates the company is solvent or that a contingent surplus would be available; a shareholder of a parent company has no standing to oppose petitions against subsidiaries in which he holds no shares.

enrichment.short_title: Victimisation compensation where fair dismissal dominated
key_facts: Birmingham City Council dismissed Mr Lisk-Carew for gross misconduct after repeated failure to comply with management directions and sickness management policy.
An Employment Tribunal found victimisation under section 2 because protected race discrimination allegations had a significant influence on dismissal, but also found the dismissal fair.
At the remedies hearing the tribunal awarded £5,000 for injury to feelings but no loss of earnings, holding employment loss was caused by the fair dismissal not the victimisation.
Permission to appeal was limited to the tension between victimisation and fair dismissal findings.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal appeal from Employment Appeal Tribunal dismissal of remedies appeal following earlier merits finding of victimisation.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; £5,000 injury to feelings award upheld; no compensation for loss of employment because fair dismissal was the effective and dominant cause.
enrichment.ratio: Where a tribunal finds both victimisation and a fair dismissal for separate misconduct, compensation under section 57 Race Relations Act 1976 requires causation of the loss claimed; if the claimant would have been fairly dismissed absent the protected acts, loss of employment is not attributable to victimisation.

enrichment.short_title: Car surveillance recordings and RIPA interception definition
key_facts: Police placed an authorised listening device in the accused's car during a drugs conspiracy investigation, recording conversations over several weeks.
Recordings included speech between occupants and the accused's side of mobile telephone calls while in the car.
The accused argued mobile call recordings were unlawful interceptions under RIPA section 1, rendering all device evidence inadmissible under section 17.
The trial judge had ruled the evidence admissible at a section 29 preparatory hearing.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Interlocutory appeal under section 35 CPIA 1996 before trial on admissibility of surveillance recordings.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; recording the accused's spoken words into a mobile telephone from sound waves in the car is not 'interception' under RIPA; section 78 exclusion refused.
enrichment.ratio: Under RIPA section 2, interception requires making the contents of a communication available during transmission through a telecommunications system; a device that records the speaker's voice in the car captures sound waves independently of the system and is not interception even when words are simultaneously transmitted by mobile phone.

Application of section 17 RIPA exclusion to surveillance device evidence

enrichment.short_title: Telewest bondholder scheme class composition and FX rate
key_facts: Telewest Communications PLC and subsidiary Telewest Finance (Jersey) Ltd sought creditor schemes to restructure about $4.5 billion of defaulted bond debt through a debt-for-equity swap into Telewest Global Inc.
Sterling and dollar bondholders would receive new shares pro rata after converting all claims to US dollars using an Average Exchange Rate from October 2002 to the explanatory statement date.
A minority committee of sterling bondholders objected that the Average Exchange Rate disadvantaged them relative to a spot rate on the valuation date.
Telewest was heavily insolvent and the scheme was proposed as an alternative to liquidation following a stayed winding-up petition.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Section 425(1) application for leave to convene creditor scheme meetings under the Practice Statement following Re Hawk Insurance.
enrichment.outcome: Leave granted to convene single creditor class meetings for both schemes; sterling and dollar bondholders held to form one class despite FX conversion dispute; fairness of Average Exchange Rate reserved for sanction hearing.
enrichment.ratio: At the convening stage the court determines class composition by comparing creditors' rights under the scheme with rights in the relevant insolvency counterfactual; currency conversion at a valuation date is part of the pari passu distribution mechanism in liquidation, but differences in financial outcome from an average versus spot rate do not automatically require separate scheme classes unless rights are so dissimilar that creditors cannot consult together.
legal_issues: Whether sterling and dollar bondholders constitute separate scheme classes
Whether Average Exchange Rate departs from creditors' liquidation rights materially enough to require separate meetings
Composition of class including subsidiary creditor Telewest Jersey
Validity of bondholder voting agreements at scheme meeting stage
